extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners learning scientific/experimental method (philosophy of science, experimentalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to discover laws and causation by direct induction: mental decomposition of phenomena, the distinction between observation and experiment, and the four experimental methods (Agreement, Difference, Joint/Indirect, and elimination-based reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying the circumstances (Baconian rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must be able to meet with some of the antecedents apart from the rest, and observe what follows from them; or some of the consequents, and observe by what they are preceded. We must, in short, follow the Baconian rule of varying the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the first rule of physical inquiry and the foundation of other methods: deliberately change or compare circumstances to detect which are connected with a phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental subdivision to points requiring observation/experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The only object of the mental separation is to suggest the requisite physical separation ... we have done enough when we have carried the subdivision as far as the point at which we are able to see what observations or experiments we require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose complex phenomena mentally until you can identify specific observations or experiments to perform; remain ready to carry decomposition further and avoid being constrained by ordinary classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Observation vs Experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of varying the circumstances, we may have recourse either to observation or to experiment ... There is no difference in kind, no real logical distinction, between the two processes of investigation. There are, however, practical distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments extend observation by producing many and precise variations not supplied by nature; observation is necessary where artificial production is impossible. Use experiment where you can produce controlled variations; rely on observation when you cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of artificial production and insulation of phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: When we can produce a phenomenon artificially, we can take it, as it were, home with us, and observe it in the midst of circumstances with which in all other respects we are accurately acquainted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificially producing a phenomenon allows control of concomitant circumstances and successive introduction of well-defined changes (examples: electric machine for lightning phenomena, Leyden jar, voltaic battery, chemists isolating substances before testing reactions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation alone cannot prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation, in short, without experiment (supposing no aid from deduction) can ascertain sequences and co-existences, but can not prove causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even invariable antecedence found by comparing observed instances does not establish unconditional causation unless the antecedent can be produced and the consequent observed to follow under known circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of reversing the process (produce antecedent to confirm cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose that, by a comparison of cases of the effect, we have found an antecedent which appears to be, and perhaps is, invariably connected with it: we have not yet proved that antecedent to be the cause until we have reversed the process, and produced the effect by means of that antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To complete induction and establish causation, produce the putative cause under controlled circumstances and verify that the effect follows (example: producing crystallization from liquid state).

rubrics_metrics.name: First Canon / Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: First Canon. If two or more instances of the phenomenon under investigation have only one circumstance in common, the circumstance in which alone all the instances agree, is the cause (or effect) of the given phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare diverse instances in which the phenomenon occurs; any single circumstance common to all is an invariable antecedent or consequent. Useful for suggesting candidate causes or laws, especially where experimentation is impracticable (example: soaps from alkali + oil combinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Canon / Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Second Canon. If an instance in which the phenomenon under investigation occurs, and an instance in which it does not occur, have every circumstance in common save one, that one occurring only in the former; the circumstance in which alone the two instances differ, is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a case where the phenomenon occurs with a nearly identical case where it does not. This method is particularly tied to experiment and affords stronger evidence for causation (example: comparing A B C → a b c with B C → b c yields a as effect of A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference requires strict identity of other circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The two instances which are to be compared with one another must be exactly similar, in all circumstances except the one which we are attempting to investigate: they must be in the relation of A B C and B C, or of a b c and b c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because nature rarely yields perfectly matched spontaneous instances, this method is most practicable in controlled experiments where one definite change can be introduced rapidly into a known pre-existing state; beware that methods of producing the change might themselves introduce effects (test by additional experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement is eliminative but weaker for causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement stands on the ground that whatever can be eliminated, is not connected with the phenomenon by any law. The Method of Agreement leads only to laws of phenomena ... The Method of Agreement is chiefly to be resorted to ... as an inferior resource, in case the Method of Difference is impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement finds invariable antecedents/consequents but cannot by itself determine causation; it is valuable for suggesting which antecedent to try with the Method of Difference or when experimentation is impossible (e.g., astronomy, mental and social sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference (Joint Method of Agreement and Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: This method may be called the Indirect Method of Difference, or the Joint Method of Agreement and Difference; and consists in a double employment of the Method of Agreement, each proof being independent of the other, and corroborating it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that all instances where a occurs contain A (agreement), and all instances where a does not occur lack A (agreement on absence); together these positive and negative agreements simulate the direct Difference method when direct removal/production experiments are impossible (example: inferring crystalline structure connection to double refraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of elimination (successive exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of discovering and proving laws of nature ... proceeds on the following axiom: Whatever circumstances can be excluded, without prejudice to the phenomenon, or can be absent notwithstanding its presence, is not connected with it in the way of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically exclude concomitants; if only one circumstance remains after elimination it is the likely cause; if more than one remain, they contain or are the cause. This underlies Agreement and Difference methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and cautions about hidden/complex antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is found invariable with a, it may not be the unconditional antecedent but may precede it as day precedes night ... It is hardly ever possible to ascertain all the antecedents ... we may overlook some of the material circumstances in an experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize epistemic limits: in complex/natural phenomena (human mind, societies, zoology) inability to isolate antecedents makes causal inference uncertain; even experiments can miss hidden causal factors (example: pumps and atmospheric pressure).

rubrics_metrics.name: When experiments are impossible, deduction plays a larger role
rubrics_metrics.description: In the sciences which deal with phenomena in which artificial experiments are impossible ... induction from direct experience is practiced at a disadvantage ... the methods of those sciences ... must be to a great extent, if not principally, deductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fields like astronomy, mental philosophy, social science, and some physiology often require deductive methods supplemented by observation because controlled experimental manipulation is limited or impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that means used to introduce a change may themselves cause effects
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one doubt, indeed, which may remain in some cases of this description; the effect may have been produced not by the change, but by the means employed to produce the change. The possibility, however, of this last supposition generally admits of being conclusively tested by other experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing Difference experiments, test whether the instrument or procedure used to effect the change contributes to observed effects by running additional controls or alternative methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Agreement to handle inseparable combinations of antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: When the agency by which we can produce the phenomenon is not that of one single antecedent, but a combination of antecedents, which we have no power of separating from each other ... the only mode ... is that afforded by the Method of Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot separate a compound cause (e.g., properties of a particular substance), compare multiple distinct instances that produce the phenomenon to find a common property (example: double refraction linked to crystallinity through comparison across substances).
